title: THE WOMEN MEN DESTROYED IN THE BIBLE — AND THE SAVIOR WHO REFUSED TO LEAVE THEM IN THE RUINS
paragraphs: THE WOMEN MEN DESTROYED IN THE BIBLE — AND THE SAVIOR WHO REFUSED TO LEAVE THEM IN THE RUINS

They were violated, used, traded, abandoned, silenced, blamed, and sometimes left without even a name. The Bible does not hide what sinful men did to women. It records the wreckage—and then leads us to Jesus Christ, the Man who never used a woman for His pleasure, never exploited her weakness, never confused lust with love, and never walked past her pain.
There is a woman lying at a doorway.
Before you read another sentence, see her.
Not as a Bible character.
Not as an illustration for a sermon.
As a woman.
Somebody's daughter.
A human being made in the image of God.
She has spent the night being brutalized by men while another man—the man who should have protected her—survived inside.
Morning comes.
The door opens.
She is there.
Her hands are at the threshold.
And Scripture gives us one of the most horrifying sentences in the Bible:
“Get up; let us be going.”
But there is no answer.
Judges 19 is not comfortable Christianity.
It is not a verse embroidered on a pillow.
It is Scripture dragging human depravity into the light and refusing to let religious people pretend evil becomes less evil merely because it happened thousands of years ago.
The Hebrew calls this woman an אִשָּׁה פִילֶגֶשׁ — ishshah pilegesh — a woman, a concubine.
Her personal name is never given.
That may be one of the most haunting details of all.
We know the Levite.
We know where he came from.
We know where they traveled.
We know what the men wanted.
We know what happened afterward.
But we do not know her name.
And perhaps that is why her story still sounds terrifyingly modern.
Because history is full of women whose pain everybody discussed while nobody remembered the woman.
Women reduced to scandals.
Women remembered by what was done to them.
Women whose stories became gossip before they became grief.
Women whose bodies became battlefields for the sins of powerful people.
And the Bible does not look away.
Neither should we.
But understand something before going further.
This is not an article declaring men evil and women innocent.
That would not be Christianity.
The Gospel says something far more devastating.
“All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
Women sin.
Men sin.
Women can abuse power. Men can abuse power.
Hagar herself was treated harshly by Sarai, a woman.
Sin does not belong to one sex.

But Scripture contains particular stories in which women suffered terribly through the lust, cowardice, selfishness, violence, negligence, or abuse of men—and those stories deserve to be heard without being softened to protect our comfort.
Because somewhere reading this is a woman who knows what it feels like to become collateral damage in somebody else's appetite.
And somewhere reading this is a man who needs enough courage to ask whether he has ever wounded a woman while calling what he felt “love.”
That question takes us into a royal house.
Her name was Tamar.
She was beautiful.
She was a daughter of David.
A princess.
And Amnon said he loved her.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 13:1 says:
וַיֶּאֱהָבֶהָ אַמְנוֹן
wayye'ehaveha Amnon.
Amnon “loved her.”
But keep reading.
Because the Bible is about to expose one of the most dangerous counterfeits of love.
Amnon becomes consumed with Tamar.
He wants access to her.
He schemes.
He manipulates circumstances.
He gets her alone.
Tamar realizes what is happening and begs him not to do it.
She reasons with him.
She resists him.
He refuses to listen.
And because he is stronger than she is, he violates her.
Then comes one of Scripture's most psychologically brutal observations.
After taking what he wanted, Amnon's supposed love becomes hatred.
The Hebrew text says:
הַשִּׂנְאָה ... מֵאַהֲבָה
ha-sin'ah ... me-ahavah.
The hatred with which he hated her became greater than the “love” with which he had loved her.
Read that slowly.
Because Scripture just exposed lust wearing love's clothing.
Real love does not destroy the person it claims to desire.
Real love does not say, “If you love me, prove it with your body.”
Real love does not manipulate vulnerability.
Real love does not punish boundaries.
Real love does not become hatred when denied gratification.
Real love “seeketh not her own” (1 Corinthians 13:5).
Amnon did not love Tamar as God defines love.
He desired possession.
And when desire had consumed what it wanted, the mask came off.
Then he threw her out.
Tamar went away grieving, with ashes upon her head.
The scandal belonged to Amnon.
But Tamar carried the shame.
How many women know that feeling?
Someone else sinned against you...
yet somehow you became ashamed.
He lied, but you wondered what was wrong with you.
He cheated, but you wondered whether you were beautiful enough.
He manipulated you, but you called yourself stupid.
He violated your boundaries, but you replayed the moment asking what you should have done differently.
He abandoned you, and you began treating his rejection as a verdict on your worth.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel never requires us to rename evil so that sinners can remain comfortable.
Grace is not pretending nothing happened.
Forgiveness is not calling darkness light.
And repentance is not saying, “I'm sorry you felt hurt.”
Biblical repentance faces the truth.
The Hebrew text later describes what Amnon did with the verb עִנָּה — 'innah—language associated here with humiliating, afflicting, or violating Tamar.
God did not inspire Scripture to disguise what happened.
Neither should the church.
And then there is Hagar.
An Egyptian servant in Abraham's household.
Before Hagar becomes part of a theological discussion, remember that she was a human being living under the authority of people more powerful than she was.
Genesis 16 calls her שִׁפְחָה מִצְרִית — shifchah mitzrit — an Egyptian female servant.
Sarai could not conceive and gave Hagar to Abram.
Abram agreed.
Hagar conceived.
Conflict followed.
Then Genesis records:
וַתְּעַנֶּהָ שָׂרַי
vatte'anneha Sarai.
Sarai dealt harshly with her, afflicted her, mistreated her.
Notice the Bible's honesty again.
The victimizer in this scene is a woman.
Scripture will not cooperate with simplistic gender warfare.

But Abram—the man with tremendous authority in this household—does not emerge as some spotless protector either. Hagar is caught inside decisions made by people with vastly greater power than she possesses.
Eventually she runs.
Pregnant.
Into the wilderness.
Imagine that journey.
No maternity ward.
No safety net.
No comfortable home waiting at the end of the road.
A pregnant servant running into a wilderness because the place called home had become unbearable.
And there...
God found her.
That sentence is worth everything.
God found her.
The woman other people treated as useful was not invisible to heaven.
The servant had a name before God.
The foreigner had a name before God.
The pregnant runaway had a name before God.
And Hagar eventually speaks of the God who sees her.
אֵל רֳאִי
El Roi.
The God who sees me.
Maybe you need that name of God tonight.
Because some wounds are made worse by the terrifying thought that nobody saw.
Nobody saw what happened after the door closed.
Nobody heard the things he said.
Nobody saw the messages.
Nobody knew how afraid you were.
Nobody understood why you changed.
Nobody noticed how much of yourself disappeared trying to keep someone else happy.
But God saw.
God saw Tamar.
God saw Hagar.
God saw the unnamed woman at the doorway.
God saw Dinah after Shechem violated her in Genesis 34.
God saw Bathsheba when David, the king, summoned her into a situation marked by an enormous imbalance of royal power and then arranged the death of her husband Uriah after she became pregnant.
And Scripture does something important in David's story.
When Nathan confronts David, he does not place the primary prophetic condemnation upon Bathsheba.
He points at David and says:
“Thou art the man.”
That is biblical accountability.
Not protecting the powerful because they are useful.
Not burying sin because the offender is gifted.
Not worrying more about a man's reputation than the people wounded by his choices.
“You are the man.”
Imagine what would happen if those words returned to Christian masculinity.
Not as hatred toward men.
As a call to holy men.
Men who protect instead of prey.
Men who repent instead of manipulate.
Men who can hear “no” without rage.
Men who keep covenant when temptation whispers.
Men who refuse pornography's education in objectification.
Men who do not use spiritual authority to control women.
Men who do not quote “wives, submit yourselves” while conveniently forgetting that Christlike husbands are commanded to love sacrificially as Christ loved the church.
Men who would rather crucify their lust than crucify somebody else's dignity.
Men who understand that masculinity is not proven by how many women desire you but by how faithfully your life resembles Jesus.
Because then Jesus arrives.
And suddenly the treatment of women becomes breathtaking.
A Samaritan woman stands beside a well in John 4.
Jesus knows her history.
He knows about the husbands.
He knows about the man presently in her life.
He knows everything.
And He speaks to her.
Not around her.
Not about her.
To her.
He does not pretend her story does not matter.
He tells her the truth.
But truth in the hands of Jesus is not a weapon for sadistic humiliation.
It becomes a doorway toward living water.
The woman who came carrying a water jar eventually leaves it behind and runs into the city talking about Christ.
“Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?”
The woman with a complicated past becomes a witness.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Then another woman comes crawling through a crowd.
Twelve years of bleeding.
Twelve years.
Think about what twelve years means.
Twelve years of waking up with the same problem.
Twelve years of hoping.
Twelve years of disappointment.
Twelve years of watching other people's lives move while yours seems trapped inside one relentless sentence.
She reaches for Jesus.
She touches His garment.
And the bleeding stops.
But Jesus does something more than heal her body.
He turns around.
He brings the hidden woman into the light—not to humiliate her, but to restore her.
And then He says one word that must have landed on her wounded soul like heaven itself:
Θυγάτηρ.
Thygatēr.
“Daughter.”
Daughter.
Not nuisance.
Not unclean woman.
Not embarrassing interruption.
Not damaged goods.
Daughter.
Then:
ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε
hē pistis sou sesōken se.
“Your faith has made you well”—with sesōken coming from sōzō, a word carrying the beautiful biblical field of saving, rescuing, healing, making whole.
And then:
ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην
hypage eis eirēnēn.
Go into peace.
Do you see Jesus?
This is Christianity.
Not men protecting male sin.
Not women being taught to tolerate abuse as though suffering at the hands of an unrepentant abuser were a spiritual virtue.
Not sinners weaponizing forgiveness to escape accountability.
Jesus.
Jesus touching the unclean.
Jesus dignifying women others dismissed.
Jesus receiving repentant sinners.
Jesus exposing hypocrisy.
Jesus telling truth.
Jesus forgiving sin.
Jesus restoring dignity.
Jesus making broken people whole.
And ultimately Jesus Himself being stripped, mocked, beaten, humiliated, pierced, and crucified.
Why?
Because the deepest destroyer in every one of these stories is bigger than man versus woman.
The deepest enemy is sin.
Sin corrupts desire.
Sin turns authority into domination.
Sin turns sexuality into consumption.
Sin turns people into objects.
Sin makes victims hide and perpetrators justify themselves.
And sin lives in male and female hearts alike.
That is why feminism alone cannot save us.
Masculinity movements cannot save us.
Politics cannot save us.
Self-help cannot save us.
Religious performance cannot save us.
We need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
At the cross, Christ does not merely offer traumatized people better self-esteem.
He deals with sin at its root.
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
That means there is grace for the woman who has been destroyed.
And there is grace for the man who finally admits he has been doing the destroying.
But grace does not mean remaining the same.
The Gospel says repent.
Turn.
Come into the light.
If you abused someone, repent.
If you manipulated someone sexually, repent.
If you betrayed your marriage, repent.
If pornography has trained your eyes to consume human beings made in God's image, repent.
If you use anger to intimidate your wife or girlfriend, repent.
If you weaponize Scripture to control someone, repent.
If you have treated women's bodies as commodities while singing worship songs on Sunday, repent.
Do not hide behind “God knows my heart.”
He does.
That is precisely why repentance is necessary.
And if you are the woman who was wounded, please hear something equally important.
What happened to you is not the final author of who you are.
Your abuser does not get authorship rights over the rest of your life.
Your abandonment does not name you.
Your divorce does not name you.
Your assault does not name you.
Your betrayal does not name you.
Your sexual past does not possess the authority to write the last chapter.
Your worst night cannot overrule the empty tomb.
Christ can redeem what sin devastated.
That does not mean every scar disappears overnight.
It does not mean trauma is imaginary.
It does not mean justice is unnecessary.
It does not mean reconciliation is automatically safe or required where there is continuing abuse and no repentance.
And it certainly does not mean staying in immediate danger to prove you have faith.
It means evil does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Maybe you saw Tamar and suddenly remembered yourself.
Maybe Hagar's wilderness felt familiar.
Maybe you have spent years being everybody's strong woman while quietly wondering whether God still sees you.
Maybe you are a man reading this with an uncomfortable heaviness because faces are coming into your mind.
Someone you used.
Someone you lied to.
Someone whose trust you broke.
Someone you pressured.
Someone you abandoned.
Someone who still carries a wound bearing your fingerprints.
Run toward Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Where appropriate and safe, make restitution.
Accept consequences.
Stop defending the person Jesus is calling you to crucify.
There is mercy at the cross even for people who discover that they were the villain in somebody else's story.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus saves sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Real ones.
The sexually broken.
The adulterer.
The liar.
The coward.
The manipulator.
The bitter.
The abused.
The abuser who genuinely repents.
The ashamed.
The self-righteous.
The person crying in the wilderness.
The person who caused someone else to run there.
But nobody comes to Jesus clutching both salvation and the right to remain unchanged.
Grace forgives us.
Then grace begins transforming us.
That is why this is bigger than an article about women destroyed by men.
It is about what sin does to human beings...
and what Jesus Christ can do with the ruins.
Not performative.
Not religious.
Honest.
Sometimes confession begins with four words typed through trembling fingers.
And sometimes testimony begins when somebody realizes, “I am not the only one.”
Not because every sentence will feel good tomorrow.
You may never know whose midnight prayer your share answers.
And yes, even share it with the skeptic who thinks the Bible hides human ugliness.
It doesn't.
Scripture exposes human sin with frightening honesty because the Bible's Hero is not humanity.
The Hero is Christ.
I want to be careful here because biblical truth matters more than fundraising.

Scripture teaches generous support for Gospel ministry, but it also says giving should be purposeful and willing, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

If these articles glorify Christ, proclaim His Gospel, call sinners to repentance, strengthen wounded believers, and help people open their Bibles again, your monthly support becomes a practical offering toward keeping that work moving.
Scripture recognizes the legitimacy of materially supporting Gospel ministry. Paul wrote that “the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14).
Supporting faithful Christian work can therefore be an act of generosity offered to God's glory.
Not purchasing God's favor.
Not buying a blessing.
Not paying for salvation.
You could never purchase what Jesus bought with His blood.
Salvation is grace.
But redeemed people can freely choose to put their resources behind work they believe advances the Gospel.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is another morning in Scripture.
Another conviction you needed.
Another reminder when your faith feels weak.
Another opportunity to point someone toward Jesus.
Another soul encountering the Gospel.
Because this world has enough voices teaching people how to disguise their wounds.
We need Christ teaching us how to bring them into His light.
Enough Amnons calling lust love.
Enough Davids believing power can hide consequences.
Enough Hagars running into wildernesses believing nobody sees.
Enough Tamars carrying shame that belongs to somebody else's sin.
Enough unnamed women collapsing at thresholds while everybody else keeps moving.
And enough men believing repentance makes them weak.
Repentance does not emasculate a man.
It brings a sinful man to the feet of the only perfect Man who ever lived.
Jesus Christ.
The Man who possessed all authority and never abused it.
The Man who knew every woman's secret and never exploited one.
The Man who confronted sin without becoming cruel.
The Man who defended dignity without redefining holiness.
The Man who touched the unclean.
The Man who welcomed the repentant.
The Man who carried our sin.
The Man who died our death.
The Man who walked out of His grave.
The King who still looks at ruined human stories and says:
I am not finished.
So remember the woman at the doorway.
Remember Tamar in ashes.
Remember Hagar beside the spring.
Remember the bleeding woman trembling at Jesus' feet.
And then remember what He called her.
Daughter.
That is what grace does.
Sin reduces people to bodies.
Grace restores persons.
Sin uses.
Grace gives.
Sin hides.
Grace brings truth into light.
Sin wounds.
Christ saves.
And when Jesus takes the pen, the chapter that nearly destroyed you does not have permission to become the ending.
Your wound may explain some of your scars—but only Jesus Christ has the authority to write your final sentence.
